vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning

paras: There is a moment about eight minutes into every interview when the hiring manager asks a question that sounds like small talk and is not. Tell me about your current role. Almost everybody answers it with a job title and a list, and almost nobody answers the question that was actually asked, which is: how much of this work is yours?

Sofia Rentz has been on both sides of that table for eleven years, and she says the difference between the two answers is one grammatical structure. “A title tells me what you are called,” she says. “A clause tells me what you own.” She gives the example she uses in every workshop. I am a senior accountant. Now the same person, one sentence later: I am the accountant who runs the close for Brazil, in a team that covers six countries, and I am the person the auditors come to when a number needs explaining. Same job. Completely different scope.

What that second version does, she says, is remove her own job from the interview. “I am no longer trying to work out how big your role is. You have told me. And because you told me in a clause and not in a claim, I believe it — a clause is a fact with a shape, and a claim is an adjective.” She is direct about the difference between saying you are hands-on and saying you are the person who prepares it and reviews it before anybody else sees it. One of those is an opinion about yourself. The other is a description.

The rest of her advice fits in three lines and she gives it to everybody who asks. Name one achievement with a number in it, because a number cannot be argued with. Name one strength and immediately give the evidence, in the same breath. And know your notice period before you are asked, because hesitating on the easiest question in the interview is the only one of the three that people actually remember.

listenings.text: I interview for finance roles and I will tell you the honest truth about what I am listening for, because it is not what most candidates prepare. I am not testing your accounting. Your CV already told me you can do the work, and the reference will tell me the rest. What I am working out in those forty minutes is whether you can explain something complicated to somebody who is not in your field, because that is eighty per cent of a senior finance job and it is the part nobody can teach quickly. So when you describe your current role, describe the shape of it. Who comes to you, and with what. What decision is yours and what decision is somebody else's. What happens in your process when you are on holiday. Those three answers tell me more than any qualification on the page, and almost nobody gives them.

The question that catches people is not the difficult one. It is: tell me about a strength. And almost everybody answers with an adjective. I am organised. I am detail-oriented. I am a fast learner. Those three sentences say nothing, and worse, they sound identical to the four candidates before you. What works is an adjective plus evidence, in one breath. I am the person who finds the difference before the auditor does, and last year that saved us three weeks of review. Now I have heard a strength and I have heard the proof of it, and I have not had to take your word for anything. Same with the weakness question, incidentally. Do not perform humility. Name something real, say what you are doing about it, and move on before it becomes the subject of the interview.
